deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

I can no longer trust my own body
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.item: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: Compulsive exercise is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other selected items cluster around hypervigilance, dissociation, memory disorganisation, and danger-based appraisals after terrorism. Excessive exercise does not clearly serve or connect to those symptoms, making it look like a strategy for a different presentation unless additional context were present.

issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is disproportionately severe relative to the rest of the selected profile and is not well supported by the surrounding appraisals. The other appraisals focus on danger and bodily unreliability, while the threat/memory items emphasize hyperarousal and fragmented recall. This suicidal-hopelessness appraisal can occur in PTSD, but here it stands out as insufficiently linked to the rest of the formulation and item set.

vignette: Six years ago, Valentina Reyes was waiting on Platform 4 of the central transit hub when the first explosions tore through the concourse. The violence erupted without warning. Metal shrieked, concrete dust choked the air, and strangers became a blur of panicked flight. She remembers the weight of the emergency door handle against her palm, the smell of burnt insulation, and the chaotic rush of bodies surging past her. But when the initial blasts gave way to a sudden, stunned quiet, the tapestry of those minutes frayed into blank spaces. She knows she survived, yet the gaps in those hours remain untouched, no matter how hard she presses them. In the months that followed, the missing pieces would occasionally surface as raw, unfiltered fury. When fragments of that day intruded, a hot, tight rage would flood her chest, demanding release but refusing to be named. She knew exactly what had occurred; she simply could not find the words to hold it. The terror had taught her that the world had no safe corners, a certainty that settled into her bones and refused to lift. Now twenty-four, Valentina works the night shift at a regional distribution warehouse. The concrete floor stretches under fluorescent lights, bounded by high bay shelves and heavy steel doors. She constantly scans the periphery, her eyes tracking doorways, overhead gates, and the movement of every pair of boots. When a coworker drops a scanning gun or a forklift jerks into motion, her guard snaps taut. She remains on constant alert, certain that letting her posture drop, even for a second, invites catastrophe. Her body feels like a compromised instrument; the way it tenses, the way it refuses to rest, leaves her doubting her own capacity to stay safe. When the warehouse floor grows too loud or the pressure mounts, Valentina deliberately lets her focus slip. She steps back inside her mind, watching herself from a distance as if she is no longer in her own skin. At work, she has stopped meeting anyone's eyes. Conversations become exchanges with shoulders and collars; faces are too much to hold. At night, the vigilance only deepens. Sleep is a risk she cannot take. She keeps the hallway light burning, listens to the settling of the house, and waits for morning. A dropped key or a sudden knock at the door sends her heart hammering against her ribs, her breath catching before she can force it down. The darkness outside her windows feels thick and unyielding, and she stays awake simply because night offers no guarantee of safety. Over months, these realities hardened into her daily rhythm. She turned down weekend gatherings because crowded rooms triggered the same relentless scanning. Her supervisor noted the missed breaks and the way she flinched at routine inventory counts, eventually reassigning her to a solitary stocking route. The isolation of the route matches her need to control what she sees, but it has also carved a quiet distance between her and the other night-shift workers. Friends who once called now text with cautious patience, sensing a distance they cannot cross. She does not explain the gaps, the rage, or the way she must remain armed with attention. What finally brought Valentina to this office was a shift where a pallet dropped too close to her station. Her vision narrowed to a tunnel, and she realized she had been walking through her days preparing for a war that had already ended, while the peace she was supposed to be living felt completely out of reach. She is afraid that the tension holding her together will eventually snap, that she will lose the ability to work or stay awake. Yet, beneath that fear, she hopes someone might help her understand why her own mind and body feel like adversaries, and whether it is possible to lay down the watch without collapsing.
